name: Lock-in Hall
description: Hall probe's strip with a steady current (your supply on its right end), in your solenoid swinging as $B_0 \sin(0.125\,t)$, a period of about 50 (your second supply sets $B_0$). The Hall voltage across the strip swings with the field, in step with it or against it as the current's direction says. A lock-in amplifier picks out a signal's swing at one frequency, its size and its phase, from the noise and from anything else the strip does: here the top contact against the bottom one at the field's frequency, over three periods from $t = 10$. Make its amplitude between 4.7 and 7, in step with the field (its phase between -60 and 30 degrees: it lags a little, as the contacts charge through the strip). Which way must the current flow?

reality.represents: Lock-in detection of a Hall voltage in a swinging field

remarks.line: A lock-in reads amplitude and phase
remarks.detail: Averaging the signal times the reference's sine and cosine over whole periods keeps only what swings at that frequency: the Hall voltage, not the noise, the offset or the magnetoresistance, which swings at twice the frequency.
The Hall voltage follows the field in step or against it as the current's direction and the carriers' sign say: how a lock-in reads a material's carriers.
The voltmeter contacts charge through the strip's resistance, so the reading lags the field by about 17° at this frequency, as cable capacitance shifts a real lock-in's phase.
The swinging field also induces an electric field circling the board's centre; the contacts sit on its symmetry line, so it does not reach the reading, as twisted leads keep it out of a real one.
The floating side contacts read the potential as an ideal voltmeter does, through a capacitance of 1 to ground, drawing no current.

remarks.line: A classical metal, a semiconductor by its ratios
remarks.detail: The carriers are classical particles at the lattice's temperature bouncing off fixed ion cores (the Drude model). A real metal's electrons are a degenerate quantum gas whose own ratios (plasma oscillations per collision, screening per free path) the model cannot afford; its carriers have a lightly doped semiconductor's ratios (the Scales section names which), which conducts by the same laws.

The strip is infinitely long along z, its carriers lines of charge moving as one: currents are per unit length, and the noise is larger than a real conductor's, whose carriers move independently along its length.
